items: Server verifies, creates a session record, returns an opaque ID
Cookie holds ONLY that random ID
User ID, roles, expiry all live server-side
Store is Redis, Postgres, or process memory
Each request: cookie, lookup, attach user, handle

lines: // >=128 bits, never a counter or UUIDv1

items: Logout is instant and real: delete the record
The ID becomes worthless everywhere at once
Ban a user, force-logout every device
Invalidate everything on password change
Revocation is the headline advantage
One store round trip on every single request
A shared store the moment you run two processes
In-memory stores plus sticky sessions break scaling
That is the classic 'random logouts after deploy'

blocks.title: Regenerate On Login
blocks.text: Session fixation: attacker plants an ID, victim logs in, attacker owns the session. Call `req.session.regenerate()` on login and on any privilege change.

items: Implement absolute AND idle, not one of them
Rolling without an absolute cap = sessions live forever
Set TTL at the store level or dead records accumulate

blocks.title: Fingerprint Softly
items: Store the session's IP and user-agent
Use them to flag obvious hijacking
Do not hard-bind — mobile IPs change constantly

blocks.title: Signed Cookie Sessions
blocks.text: Rails and Flask style: data lives IN the cookie under an HMAC. No store to run, but no revocation either, and the 4KB cap bites fast.

caption.text: Part 3 of HTTP COOKIES & WEB AUTH. Your session cookie is one missing attribute away from being someone else's. This field manual walks every `Set-Cookie` attribute, why `Path` silently eats your login, how a compromised subdomain can overwrite a cookie it should never touch, and where SameSite actually stops CSRF versus where it just looks like it does.
